name: Glyceryl tris-3-hydroxybutyrate

card.summary: A ketone triglyceride (3GHB) that releases beta-hydroxybutyrate; human work so far is limited to pharmacokinetic studies.
card.note: Not authorized as an EU novel food; an application is pending per the Commission summary cited.

quick.overview:
Glyceryl tris-3-hydroxybutyrate is a water-soluble oil in which glycerol carries three beta-hydroxybutyrate groups, one of the ketone bodies. It is discussed as an exogenous ketone source, in the fat-loss and metabolism category.

The human studies registered for it are pharmacokinetic studies in healthy volunteers; no efficacy trials for fat loss or appearance appear in the sources.
quick.mechanism: After ingestion the ester groups are expected to be cleaved by lipases and esterases, releasing beta-hydroxybutyrate and glycerol into the circulation, where tissues can burn the ketone.
quick.risks: A 2025 toxicology package sponsored for novel-food use reported no genotoxicity and no adverse effects in a 90-day rat study. Human safety data are limited, and the compound is the subject of a pending EU novel-food application, not an authorization.

lead: Glyceryl tris-3-hydroxybutyrate (3GHB, also tri-betahydroxybutyrin) is a synthetic triglyceride in which glycerol is fully esterified with beta-hydroxybutyric acid, a ketone body. It has the formula C15H26O9 and is a water-soluble clear oil.[1] It is not itself a ketone.[1] The appearance interest in it comes from the exogenous-ketone category: raising blood ketones without fasting or a ketogenic diet is discussed by users in connection with appetite control and fat loss, which affect how lean a person looks.[4]

Its synthesis and a seven-day infusion in rats were reported in 1997 by Birkhahn and colleagues, with support from Eastman Chemical Company, as a candidate parenteral nutrient.[1] It is discussed alongside ketone esters and salts as an exogenous ketone, a category reviewed in the context of ketone body therapy.[1][2][3][4]

After ingestion, the beta-hydroxybutyrate groups are cleaved from the glycerol backbone and enter the circulation, where tissues oxidise them for energy.[5] Human studies registered for the compound are pharmacokinetic studies in healthy volunteers, not efficacy trials.[1] No study of it for fat loss or appearance has been published.
infobox: EU novel-food application pending; not authorized

paras: After oral exposure, the beta-hydroxybutyrate groups are expected to be cleaved from the glycerol backbone by gut lipases and esterases and released into the circulation.[1] Ketone bodies can then be oxidized by peripheral tissues.[2]

Wikipedia describes exogenous ketones as ketone bodies taken as supplements, mainly beta-hydroxybutyrate, in the forms of ketone salts and ketone esters; 3GHB is listed as a triglyceride form. In one study cited there, esters produced higher blood D-BHB levels than salts, and a ketone ester drink lowered levels of the hunger hormone ghrelin.[4]

The same article notes that evidence for exogenous ketones is limited and largely from small or animal studies, and that one study of an ester precursor in athletes found no significant difference in time to fatigue.[4]

In 1997 Ronald Birkhahn, Charles McCombs, Robert Clemens and John Hubbs reported synthesizing the glycerides and a seven-day intravenous infusion in rats; a US patent the same year describes producing the water-soluble esters for use as a parenteral nutrient.[1]

A completed 2017 pharmacokinetic study in 18 men aged 60 or older compared single oral doses of three sizes, and a later crossover study compares the triester with a ketone monoester and a ketone salt in healthy adults; neither has posted results.[1] No efficacy trial for any condition is registered, and none addresses appearance or body composition.[1] Safety studies to date are laboratory and rat studies.[5]

A 2025 toxicology package in Food and Chemical Toxicology, supporting novel-food use, reported that tri-betahydroxybutyrin was non-genotoxic in bacterial reverse mutation and micronucleus assays, and that a 90-day rat dietary study found no adverse effects up to the highest dose tested, equivalent to 1193 mg/kg body weight per day in males and 1376 in females.[5] NeuroEnergy Ventures has applied to authorize it in the European Union as a novel-food ingredient for foods for special medical purposes; the Commission summary describes an ongoing application, not an authorization.[1]

timeline.event: Synthesis and rat infusion study reported by Birkhahn and colleagues; US patent issued.[1]

angle.text: Exogenous ketones are discussed as a way to get ketone effects, such as reduced appetite, without a strict ketogenic diet. 3GHB is one form of this category; its effects on fat loss have not been studied.
